questions.problem:
The inverse of the $2\times 2$ matrix $D$ is found using row operations, as shown below. Complete the process, and determine ${D}^{-1}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}[D\,|\,I] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=-{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\text{___________} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\phantom{a}} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\phantom{a}} \\ 0 & 1 & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\phantom{a}} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\phantom{a}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We write down $D$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply the standard Gauss-Jordan method to transform the matrix $D$ into the identity matrix. We perform the same row operations on both matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}[D\,|\,I] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=-{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix ${D}^{-1}$ is given by the right-hand side of our big matrix after all of the transformations have been completed. Therefore, 

$$
{D}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
Find the values of $k$ such that the vector $b$ lies in $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -3 \\ k\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We know that $b\in \text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ if there exist ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2} & =b \\ {x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -3 \\ k\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}5{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-3 \\ {x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=-3 \\ 2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=k\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}5 & 1 & -3 \\ 1 & -1 & -3 \\ 2 & -1 & k\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -3 \\ 5 & 1 & -3 \\ 2 & -1 & k\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-5{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -3 \\ 0 & 6 & 12 \\ 2 & -1 & k\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -3 \\ 0 & 6 & 12 \\ 0 & 1 & k+6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{6}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & k+6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & k+4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The third row of the augmented matrix now corresponds to the equation $0{x}_{1}+0{x}_{2}=k+4.$ Therefore, the system has a solution only if

$$
0=k+4\,⇒\,k=-4.
$$

questions.problem: A nonzero vector $⟨0,\,b,\,c⟩$ is parallel to the plane $r\cdot ⟨3,2,-1⟩=\sqrt{2}.$ What is the value of $\frac{b}{c}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We need a vector $v=⟨{t}_{1},{t}_{2},{t}_{3}⟩$ that is parallel to the given plane. 

From the equation $r\cdot ⟨3,2,-1⟩=\sqrt{2}$ of the plane, we get the normal vector $n=⟨3,2,-1⟩.$ So, $v⊥n$ and we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}v\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨{t}_{1},{t}_{2},{t}_{3}⟩\cdot ⟨3,2,-1⟩ & =0 \\ 3{t}_{1}+2{t}_{2}-{t}_{3} & =0 \\ {t}_{3} & =3{t}_{1}+2{t}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we obtain 

$$
v=⟨{t}_{1},\,{t}_{2},\,3{t}_{1}+2{t}_{2}⟩,
$$

where ${t}_{1},{t}_{2}\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ 

We are told that the first component of $v$ equals $0.$ So, we must set ${t}_{1}=0.$ 

Since $v$ is nonzero, we can pick any ${t}_{2}\ne 0.$ For example, setting ${t}_{2}=1$, we get

$$
v=⟨0,\,1,\,2⟩.
$$

Therefore, $\frac{b}{c}=\frac{1}{2}.$

questions.problem: A supplier of clothing materials looks for flaws before selling the material to customers. On average, there have been $1.7$ flaws per meter. What is the probability of finding fewer than $4$  flaws in the next meter length of the material? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places. You may assume that flaws appear independently and at a constant average rate.
questions.worked_solution:
A Poisson random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{\lambda }^{x}{e}^{-\lambda }}{x!}
$$

Let $X$ be the number of flaws in a meter length of the material. Since the average rate is $1.7$ flaws per meter, and events occur independently and at a constant average rate, the number of flaws can be modeled as a Poisson random variable with rate $\lambda =1.7,$ and we can write $X∼\text{Po}(1.7).$

So, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{1.7}^{x}{e}^{-1.7}}{x!}
$$

Therefore, the probability of finding fewer than $4$  flaws in the next meter length of the material is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<4) & =P(X\in \{0,1,2,3\}) \\  & =f(0)+f(1)+f(2)+f(3) \\  & =\frac{{1.7}^{0}{e}^{-1.7}}{0!}+\frac{{1.7}^{1}{e}^{-1.7}}{1!}+\frac{{1.7}^{2}{e}^{-1.7}}{2!}+\frac{{1.7}^{3}{e}^{-1.7}}{3!} \\  & ≈0.907\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

questions.problem:
The probability distribution of the random variable $X$ is given below. Given that $\text{E}[X]=3,$ calculate $\text{Var}[7X].$ 

| $x$ | $1$ | $2$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $\frac{1}{7}$ | $\frac{2}{7}$ | $\frac{4}{7}$ |
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that for any random variable $X$ and constant $a,$ we have

$$
\text{Var}[aX]={a}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X].
$$

In our case, $a=7.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[7X] & ={7}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =49\cdot \text{Var}[X].\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the variance of $X$ using the following formula:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}
$$

Additionally, we're given that $\text{E}[X]=3.$ 

We start by computing $\text{E}[{X}^{2}].$ Summing up the products of each value of ${X}^{2}$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={1}^{2}\cdot f(1)+{2}^{2}\cdot f(2)+{4}^{2}\cdot f(4) \\  & =1\cdot \frac{1}{7}+4\cdot \frac{2}{7}+16\cdot \frac{4}{7} \\  & =\frac{73}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{73}{7}-{3}^{2} \\  & =\frac{10}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[7X] & =49\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =49\cdot \frac{10}{7} \\  & =70.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Suppose $A$ is a $4\times 4$ matrix and $det(A)=8.$ The matrix $B$ is obtained from $A$ by applying the elementary row operations ${R}_{1}:=2{R}_{1}$ and ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{2}.$ What is the value of $det(B)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's figure out what each operation does to the determinant.

- The operation ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{2}$ involves adding a multiple of one row to another row,  so it does not change the determinant.

- The operation ${R}_{1}:=2{R}_{1}$ involves multiplying a row by $2,$ so the determinant is multiplied by $2$ as well.

Therefore, we only have to multiply the determinant by $2.$ Consequently, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B) & =2det(A) \\  & =2\cdot 8 \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$
